examples.title: Do not accept a prewritten moisture answer
examples.situation: A planter-box process card predicts 'too dry', but a real 12 cm sandy-loam sample is darker, feels cool and makes a weak ball.
reasoning: Record those actual observations and the texture, place and depth.
Compare with the texture-specific guide and perhaps another root-zone sample.
Do not mark 'too dry' merely to match the card, nor turn a weak ball into a percentage.
examples.takeaway: The moisture status needs texture-specific interpretation and trainer review; the observed evidence outranks the printed expectation.

examples.title: Too much water is not progress
examples.situation: After a small water addition, a clay teaching sample is sticky and leaves a wet stain; a student wants to add more until the simulation bar fills.
reasoning: Stop water addition and record the wet observation.
A clay ribbon or firm ball is not one universal moisture target.
The trainer resets a sample by an approved method and discusses texture, drainage and possible waterlogging.
examples.takeaway: No extra water or invented optimal percentage; describe and compare the actual sample.

examples.title: Three plants, three emitters
examples.situation: Three seedlings are not equally spaced along a one-metre planter box and the emitters have to reach each intended root zone.
reasoning: Measure the tube and mark each plant position before punching.
Check tube, punch and emitter compatibility and keep the system unpressurised during assembly.
After kit-approved connection, test all three outlets and every joint under trainer supervision.
examples.takeaway: Correct positions and a leak-free, flowing test matter more than blindly equal hole spacing.
